RESEARCH ARTICLE




Log-Sobolev inequality for near critical Ising
models

Roland Bauerschmidt                              Benoit Dagallier

DPMMS, University of Cambridge,                   Abstract
Cambridge, UK
                                                  For general ferromagnetic Ising models whose coupling
Correspondence                                    matrix has bounded spectral radius, we show that the log-

European Research Council,                        over, if the susceptibility satisfies the mean-field bound as

                                                  log-Sobolev constant depends polynomially on the distance
                                                  to the critical point and on the volume. In particular, this
                                                  applies to the Ising model on subsets of ℤ𝑑 when 𝑑 > 4.
                                                  The proof uses a general criterion for the log-Sobolev
                                                  inequality in terms of the Polchinski (renormalisation

                                                  inequality for Ising models with general external fields, the
                                                  Perron–Frobenius theorem, and the log-Sobolev inequality

1      MAIN RESULT AND PROOF

1.1       Main result

Let Λ be a finite set, and denote by (⋅, ⋅) the standard inner product on ℝΛ . For 𝐴 = (𝐴𝑥𝑦 )𝑥,𝑦∈Λ a
symmetric matrix with 𝐴𝑥𝑦 ⩽ 0 if 𝑥 ≠ 𝑦, the ferromagnetic Ising model with coupling matrix 𝐴,
inverse temperature 𝛽 ⩾ 0, and external field ℎ ∈ ℝΛ has the expectation

                                                ∑             𝛽
                                                          − (𝜎,𝐴𝜎) (ℎ,𝜎)
                                𝔼𝜇𝛽,ℎ 𝐹 ∝             𝑒    2      𝑒      𝐹(𝜎).                         (1.1)
                                            𝜎∈{±1}Λ


We assume that 𝐴 is positive definite and has spectral radius ‖𝐴‖ ⩽ 1. The positive definiteness
can always be imposed by adding a diagonal matrix (without changing the corresponding Ising
model) and ‖𝐴‖ ⩽ 1 corresponds to a normalisation of the inverse temperature parameter.
   For 𝑥 ∈ Λ, let 𝜎𝑥 ∈ {±1}Λ be the spin configuration obtained from 𝜎 ∈ {±1}Λ by flipping the
sign of 𝜎𝑥 . The standard (Glauber) Dirichlet form associated with the Ising model (1.1) is

                                            1∑         [                 ]
                                                                       2
                             𝐷𝜇𝛽,ℎ (𝐹) =          𝔼𝜇𝛽,ℎ (𝐹(𝜎) − 𝐹(𝜎𝑥 )) .                              (1.2)
                                            2 𝑥∈Λ

The log-Sobolev constant 𝛾𝛽,ℎ is the largest constant such that, for all nonnegative 𝐹,

                                                          2               (√ )
                                   Ent𝜇𝛽,ℎ (𝐹) ⩽                  𝐷𝜇𝛽,ℎ     𝐹 ,                        (1.3)
                                                      𝛾𝛽,ℎ

where Ent𝜇𝛽,ℎ (𝐹) = 𝔼𝜇𝛽,ℎ Φ(𝐹) − Φ(𝔼𝜇𝛽,ℎ 𝐹) with Φ(𝑥) = 𝑥 log 𝑥 is the relative entropy. Our main
result is stated in terms of the 0-field susceptibility of the Ising model, given by
                                                    ∑
                                      𝜒𝛽 = sup                𝔼𝛽,0 (𝜎𝑥 𝜎𝑦 ).                           (1.4)
                                                𝑥∈Λ 𝑦∈Λ


Theorem 1.1. The log-Sobolev constant of (1.1) satisfies

                                                           𝛽
                                       1        1         𝑡
                                            ⩽     +  𝑒2 ∫0 𝜒𝑠 𝑑𝑠 𝑑𝑡.                                   (1.5)
                                     𝛾𝛽,ℎ       2 ∫0

  The Dirichlet form is associated with a Markov process (Glauber dynamics), see [26] for back-
ground. The standard Dirichlet form (1.2) corresponds to a convenient choice of transition rates,
but other common choices of rates (such as heat-bath and Metropolis dynamics) are equivalent
when the rates are bounded, as is the case for the standard Ising model on Λ ⊂ ℤ𝑑 , also see [26].
The log-Sobolev inequality can be equivalently formulated in terms of hypercontractivity of the
Glauber semigroup and has many well-known implications. In particular, the inverse log-Sobolev
constant bounds the relaxation rate to equilibrium in the sense of relative entropy, that is, if 𝐹𝑡 𝜇𝛽,ℎ
denotes the law of the dynamics at time 𝑡 ⩾ 0, then

                                  Ent𝜇𝛽,ℎ (𝐹𝑡 ) ⩽ 𝑒−2𝛾𝛽,ℎ 𝑡 Ent𝜇𝛽,ℎ (𝐹0 ).                             (1.6)
LOG-SOBOLEV INEQUALITY FOR NEAR CRITICAL ISING MODELS                                                3



The inverse log-Sobolev constant can also be used to obtain bounds on other notions of conver-
gence to equilibrium in finite and infinite volume, see the references [20, 25–27] for introductions
to the general implications.
   Since 𝜒𝑠 is increasing in 𝑠 (by the second Griffiths inequality), Theorem 1.1 shows in particular
that whenever 𝜒𝛽 is bounded, the log-Sobolev constant is bounded below:

                                            1         1
                                                  ⩽     + 𝛽𝑒2𝛽𝜒𝛽 .                             (1.7)
                                           𝛾𝛽,ℎ       2

This shows that the log-Sobolev inequality holds uniformly in the volume in the entire high
temperature phase of the Ising model, for example, on Λ ↑ ℤ𝑑 but equally in a much more gen-
eral setting. For lattices Λ, uniformity in the volume was recently proved in [15] by establishing
the strong spatial mixing property, see [26]. Our more general criterion does not rely on geom-
etry or mixing conditions. The new correlation inequality from [15] is also important in our
proof.
   But even more interestingly, the bound (1.5) shows that if the susceptibility satisfies the mean-
field bound then the log-Sobolev constant is polynomial (in the distance to the critical point and
in the volume). This is summarised in the following corollary, whose proof simply consists of
carrying out the integrals in (1.5) using the assumed bound on 𝜒𝛽 .

Corollary 1.2. Let 𝐷 > 1∕2 and assume that the mean-field bound 𝜒𝛽 ⩽ 𝐷∕(𝛽𝑐 − 𝛽) for all 𝛽 < 𝛽𝑐
holds. Then

               1    1   𝛽𝑐 [                    ]        𝛽𝑐
                   ⩽ +       (1 − 𝛽∕𝛽𝑐 )1−2𝐷 − 1 ∼           (1 − 𝛽∕𝛽𝑐 )1−2𝐷 .                 (1.8)
              𝛾𝛽,ℎ  2 2𝐷 − 1                      𝛽→𝛽𝑐 2𝐷 −1

Similarly, if the finite-volume mean-field bound 𝜒𝛽 ⩽ 𝐷∕(𝛽𝑐 − 𝛽 + 𝐿−2 ) for all 𝛽 < 𝛽𝑐 holds, then

               1          1 𝛽𝑐 + 𝐿−2 [ 2                ]       𝛽𝑐
                      ⩽     +         (𝐿 𝛽𝑐 + 1)2𝐷−1 − 1 ∼           (𝐿2 𝛽𝑐 + 1)2𝐷−1 .         (1.9)
             𝛾𝛽𝑐 ,ℎ       2   2𝐷 − 1                      𝐿→∞ 2𝐷 − 1


   The mean-field bound holds for Ising models on ℤ𝑑 in 𝑑 ⩾ 5, see [1, 2], and the finite-volume
mean-field bound similarly holds for the Ising model on a hypercube of side length 𝐿 (with free
boundary conditions) in 𝑑 ⩾ 5, and with possibly a different exponent for other boundary condi-
tions, see [12] for discussion of this. The exponents above are not the expected optimal ones when
Λ ↑ ℤ𝑑 , which would be −1 respectively +1 in 𝑑 ⩾ 5. We remark though that in the actual mean-
field model (the Curie–Weiss model), the mean-field bound holds with 𝐷 = 1 (see, for example
[8, Chapter 1]) and one can thus obtain the optimal exponent from (1.5). However, for the Curie–
Weiss model, also many other methods give sharp results, see, for example [26, 28], and the more
recent spectral conditions [3, 5, 17].
   For lattices, by contrast, a polynomial bound on the spectral gap for the Glauber dynamics of
the Ising model at the critical temperature has previously only been proved in two dimensions
[24]. The proof of this bound relies on the RSW estimates [16] as input. Similar estimates have
also been obtained for two-dimensional 𝑞-state Potts models with 𝑞 < 4, see [18]. The approach
of the critical point for these models appears to remain open. Other polynomial bounds for
near critical spin models were restricted to simpler geometries such as trees [14] or hierarchical
lattices [6].
4                                                                              BAUERSCHMIDT and DAGALLIER



   For completeness, we also comment briefly on the low-temperature phase, in which our tech-
nique to prove Theorem 1.1 does not seem directly useful. In this region, the Glauber dynamics
equilibrates at a rate that typically vanishes with the size of Λ (assuming the external field ℎ is
0). For the ferromagnetic Ising model in a hypercube Λ ⊂ ℤ𝑑 of side length 𝐿, boundary condi-
tions play a crucial role, and their influence is not captured by the zero-field susceptibility (1.4)
(zero field corresponds to free boundary conditions). For instance, for free boundary conditions, it
is known that the spectral gap (which is always larger than the log-Sobolev constant 𝛾𝛽,ℎ ) decays
           𝑑−1
like 𝑒−𝑐(𝛽)𝐿 (1+𝑜𝐿 (1)) when 𝛽 > 𝛽𝑐 ; the constant 𝑐(𝛽) is explicit in dimension two [26] and there are
more general bounds in dimension three and higher [10]. Conversely, if the boundary condition
is all +, there is a long-standing conjecture, the so-called Lifshitz law, that convergence to equilib-
rium from a worst-case initial condition should typically take a time of order 𝐿2 , up to logarithmic
corrections. Arguments supporting that bound are given in [11], but so far the bound has only been
established at 0 temperature in all dimensions 𝑑 ⩾ 2, see [13] in dimension 𝑑 = 2, 3 and [21] in
higher dimension. For 𝛽 ∈ (𝛽𝑐 , ∞), the currently best known results are in dimension two, where
                                                                ′
the rate of relaxation is known to be going to 0 at least as 𝐿−𝑐 (𝛽) log 𝐿 for some 𝑐′ (𝛽) > 0, see [23] and
references therein. Similar bounds can also be obtained with periodic boundary conditions instead
of all +, but for well chosen initialisations of the dynamics: bounds on the mixing time of order
                                   ′      𝑑−1
𝐿−1 in dimension 𝑑 = 2 and 𝐿𝑐 (𝛽) log 𝐿 in higher dimensions have recently been established
in [19].
    In [9], we derive a variant of Theorem 1.1 for 𝜑4 models and use it to prove that the continuum
𝜑2 and 𝜑34 measures satisfy log-Sobolev inequalities uniformly in the regularisation (and volume
  4

in the uniqueness phase).

Remark 1.3. The proof only uses that 𝜒𝛽 defined in (1.4) provides an upper bound on the spectral
radius of the two-point function (𝔼𝜇𝛽,0 (𝜎𝑥 𝜎𝑦 ))𝑥,𝑦∈Λ . Thus replacing 𝜒𝛽 by the spectral radius of
the two-point function gives a slightly more general statement.


1.2       Proof of Theorem 1.1

The strategy of the proof is to decompose 𝜇𝛽,ℎ into two measures: an infinite-temperature
Ising part, for which the log-Sobolev inequality is known; and a continuous part for which
the log-Sobolev inequality is established via the criterion based on the Polchinski (renormali-
sation group) equation from [7, Theorem 2.5]. The first part is similar to the one in [5] where
the same kind of decomposition was performed. In [5], the second part was treated with the
Bakry–Emery criterion, leading to the condition 𝛽 < 1 (but without assuming the coupling
matrix 𝐴 is ferromagnetic). In contrast, our use of the more powerful Polchinski equation cri-
terion does not require an upper bound on 𝛽. To verify the assumptions of the criterion we
exploit that 𝐴 is ferromagnetic by using the FKG inequality and the new correlation inequality
from [15].

Proof of Theorem 1.1. By taking a limit at the end, we can assume ‖𝐴‖ < 1 so that all covariances
below are nondegenerate. Fix 𝛼 > 𝛽 and define for 𝑡 ∈ [0, 𝛽]:

                                         𝐶𝑡 = (𝑡𝐴 + (𝛼 − 𝑡))−1 .                                      (1.10)

To be precise, in [7, Theorem 2.5], the covariances 𝐶𝑡 are parametrised by 𝑡 ∈ [0, ∞] rather than
𝑡 ∈ [0, 𝛽], and start at 𝐶0 = 0. This difference simply corresponds to the change of variable from 𝑡
to 𝛽(1 − 𝑒−𝑡 ) in the definition of 𝐶𝑡 , and to replacing 𝐶𝑡 by 𝐶𝑡 − 𝐶0 . We prefer the parametrisation
by 𝑡 ∈ [0, 𝛽] here due to its more transparent interpretation as a change in inverse temperature.
